4:["$","h1",null,{"className":"text-[20px] font-bold uppercase tracking-tight text-ink","children":"What Is Delta E (ΔE)?"}]
5:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":["Delta E is the number that answers the question every printer, designer, and paint matcher eventually asks: ",["$","em",null,{"children":"how different are these two colors, really?"}]," Not \"are they different\" — your eye can answer that some of the time — but by how much, on a scale where a 2 is a 2 whether you're comparing two navy inks or two skin tones. ΔE is the unit of that scale: the measured distance between two colors in a space designed to mirror human vision."]}]
6:["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-[15px] font-bold uppercase tracking-wide text-ink mt-10 pt-6 border-t border-hairline","children":"CIELAB: The Map Delta E Measures On"}]
7:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":["To measure a distance you need a map, and the map ΔE uses is ",["$","strong",null,{"children":"CIELAB"}]," (also written L*a*b*), published by the CIE in 1976. It describes any color with three coordinates:"]}]
8:["$","ul",null,{"className":"mt-4 list-disc pl-5 space-y-2 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":[["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"L*"}]," — lightness, from 0 (black) to 100 (white)"]}],["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"a*"}]," — the green–red axis: negative values lean green, positive lean red"]}],["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"b*"}]," — the blue–yellow axis: negative values lean blue, positive lean yellow"]}]]}]
9:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":["The point of CIELAB is ",["$","strong",null,{"children":"perceptual uniformity"}],": it was built so that one unit of distance anywhere on the map should look like roughly the same amount of difference to a human observer. That's what RGB can't give you — in RGB, a jump of 10 units might be invisible in one region and glaring in another, because RGB describes how much light a screen emits, not how a person sees. Converting a color to CIELAB is like converting raw pixels into the eye's own bookkeeping. Once two colors sit on this map, the difference between them becomes geometry."]}]
a:["$","h2",null,{"className":"text-[15px] font-bold uppercase tracking-wide text-ink mt-10 pt-6 border-t border-hairline","children":"Why CIEDE2000 Is Fairer Than ΔE76"}]
b:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":["The original formula, ",["$","strong",null,{"children":"ΔE76"}],", is just straight-line Euclidean distance in CIELAB: simple, fast, and honestly not bad. The problem is that CIELAB turned out to be only ",["$","em",null,{"children":"approximately"}]," uniform. Careful testing showed systematic mismatches:"]}]
c:["$","ul",null,{"className":"mt-4 list-disc pl-5 space-y-2 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":[["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"The eye tolerates bigger chroma differences in vivid colors."}]," Two saturated reds can be further apart than two grays before anyone notices. ΔE76 treats both gaps identically; CIEDE2000 adds a chroma weighting term that forgives distance in high-chroma regions and tightens tolerance near neutrals."]}],["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"The eye is stricter about lightness in mid-tones."}]," CIEDE2000's lightness weighting reflects that sensitivity curve."]}],["$","li",null,{"children":[["$","strong",null,{"children":"Blues misbehave."}]," Around the blue region, hue differences interact with chroma in a way a plain distance can't capture, so CIEDE2000 adds a rotation term (R",["$","sub",null,{"children":"T"}],") that twists the calculation there."]}]]}]
d:["$","p",null,{"className":"mt-4 text-[15px] leading-[1.75] text-ink","children":["CIEDE2000 (ΔE00) keeps the same three-part skeleton — lightness, chroma, hue — but wraps each in a weighting function derived from real perceptual experiments. The result: its numbers track trained human judgement far more consistently. When a proofreader and a press operator disagree about whether a job matches, ΔE00 is the arbiter the industry reaches for. It's what this lab uses, with the standard reference conditions (D65 illuminant, k",["$","sub",null,{"children":"L"}]," = k",["$","sub",null,{"children":"C"}]," = k",["$","sub",null,{"children":"H"}]," = 1)."]}]
